plimsoll trainer · 11 / backpressure

The capacity endpoint

When a customer's API starts returning 503 under load, the code in the sandbox keeps calling it, because it is untrusted code and cannot be relied on to back off. The broker is the one thing on the wire that both sees the distress signal and controls the next call, so it sheds. What it cannot know on its own is when to stop shedding. That is what a cheap, honest health route is for.

01

Eighty calls into a two-second outage

One brokered call every 100 ms for eight seconds. The upstream is overloaded from 0.5 s to 2.5 s and answers every forwarded call in that window with the status you choose. The breaker's rules below are the daemon's own constants: a 1 s cooldown when the upstream gives no Retry-After, any Retry-After honoured up to 30 s, one health probe per second while shedding, and none after a 429.

The upstream answers

with Retry-After

The profile declares health_check

forwarded, 2xx forwarded, overloaded reply shed: fast local 503, never forwarded probe, not ready probe, 2xx: breaker closes

02

Two statuses, two recoveries

Both open the breaker. They close differently, because the health route can answer only one of their questions.

503: the service is degraded

The question is "can the service take traffic again?", which is exactly what a readiness route reports. So while shedding, one elected caller per second sends a GET to the declared route, host-side, with the run's own credential. The probe is not traced and not charged to the run's call budget, and a hung route is abandoned after 2 s. The first 2xx closes the breaker on the spot.

429: this caller spent its allowance

The question is "has my quota reset?", and a healthy service says nothing about that. A 2xx from the health route would reopen the gate and push the run's traffic straight back into the limiter that asked it to wait. So a 429 window is never probed: it is waited out, for the Retry-After the upstream gave or the default. A window opened by a 429 keeps that property even if a 503 extends it.

Everything here is scoped to one run. One run's breaker never sheds another run's calls, and a shed is recorded as Shed in the run's call trace, distinct from a policy Denied, and surfaced as host_calls_shed on the audit line. The guest sees a 503 either way; the difference is that a shed one cost the upstream nothing.

03

Which route to probe

A 2xx has to mean "ready for traffic", and nothing else. Four routes an API might already have, and what each one's 2xx actually promises.

GET /livez, /ping weak

Promises the process is running. A live process can be shedding load; this route stays 2xx all through an overload, so the breaker would close into the fire.

GET /readyz, /health good

Promises the service can serve. Flips to non-2xx under load and back on recovery, which is the whole signal.

GET /status, /capacity best

The same readiness answer plus headroom: queue depth, remaining rate budget. The breaker uses the status line; your own dashboards can use the body.

GET /items, a real query avoid

One expensive request succeeded. Polling it once a second is a second thing to overload, and it can pass while the API is still fragile.

04

Designing the route the broker will trust

These are the properties that make a route's 2xx mean "ready". Untick the fourth and trace it: the first probe answers 2xx, the breaker closes, the run resumes into the still-struggling API, and the next call trips it again.

05

Wired from the OpenAPI document, not by hand

plimsoll-specgen derives the profile's route list and the guest SDK from one OpenAPI document. The health route comes from the same document, so adopting backpressure is one tag and one field.

  1. Tag the operation.Only the extension designates a probe. A path called /status or /healthz is not evidence of what it measures, and a probe that answers 200 for the wrong reason reopens the gate onto a struggling API.
    get:
  summary: Readiness and headroom
  x-plimsoll-health-check: true
  2. specgen refuses the wrong shape.A tag on a non-GET or on a path with a parameter fails generation closed, and two tagged routes are an error rather than a guess.
  3. One line comes out.Beside the route list, the preamble and the tool description, the generator writes a one-line health file, only when the document tags a route.
    plimsoll-specgen -emit health   # GET /status
  4. The profile gets the field.Paste it as health_check in the grant profile. The routes and the SDK came from the same document, so nothing is mirrored by hand and nothing drifts.
